questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `apply` runs the block on the receiver and returns the receiver, so `a` is the StringBuilder now holding "xy". `let` returns the lambda's result, "xy", whose length is 2. Neither function discards the change made in its block.

questions.question: You want to log an object in the middle of a call chain without changing the value that flows through the chain. Which scope function fits best?
questions.explanation: `also` passes the object as `it` and returns the same object, so it is made for side effects such as logging or validation in a chain. `let` and `run` return the lambda's result, so a logging call at the end would replace the value with `Unit`. `with` is not an extension and does not chain.

Extensions do not override each other; only member functions are dispatched virtually.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: When a member and an extension have the same signature, the member always wins and the extension is shadowed (the compiler warns about it). An extension with a different signature is a separate overload, so `show(1)` calls the extension. Extensions can add overloads but cannot replace members.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `x.also { }` captures the current value of `x` (1) as its receiver and returns that value, even though the block changes the variable to 10. The `let` then gets `it = 1` and reads the variable `x`, which is now 10, so `y` is 11. `also` returns the object it was called on, not whatever the variable holds later.

questions.question: A top-level extension function declared outside a class can access that class's `private` members.
questions.explanation: An extension is compiled to a static function that takes the receiver as a parameter, so it only sees what any outside code can see. It cannot access private or protected members. To reach private state you need a member function or an extension declared inside the class.

questions.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: `with` is not an extension function; it takes the receiver as an argument
`also` returns the result of its lambda
`let` refers to the object as `this` inside the block
`run` exists both as an extension (`x.run { }`) and as a non-extension (`run { }`)
questions.explanation: `apply` and `also` return the receiver; `let`, `run` and `with` return the lambda's result. `with(obj) { }` takes the object as a normal argument, and `run { }` without a receiver is just a block that returns a value. `let` and `also` use `it`; `apply`, `run` and `with` use `this`.

questions.question: In a type-safe HTML builder, `table { tr { tr { } } }` compiles because the inner block can still see the outer `table` receiver. How do you stop that?
options: Declare each builder lambda parameter as `crossinline`, which removes implicit access to enclosing receivers
Make all builder functions `inline`, so the outer receiver is no longer in scope inside nested lambdas
Annotate the builder classes with your own `@DslMarker` annotation; outer receivers then need `this@label`
Make the builder classes `private`, so a nested block can only call functions on its own receiver
questions.explanation: When implicit receivers come from classes that share a `@DslMarker` annotation, only the closest one can be used implicitly. Reaching an outer one needs an explicit label such as `this@table`, so mistakes like nested `tr` stop compiling. `inline` and `crossinline` control inlining and returns, not which receivers are visible.

questions.question: Why is `init` declared as `HTML.() -> Unit` instead of `(HTML) -> Unit`?
options: A receiver lambda can access the private members of `HTML`, which a regular lambda cannot
`(HTML) -> Unit` cannot be called with a trailing lambda, so the builder syntax would not work
Inside the lambda `this` is the HTML, so callers write `body { }` without a parameter name
A receiver lambda is always inlined by the compiler, so it avoids allocating a function object
questions.explanation: A function type with receiver makes the argument the implicit `this` inside the lambda, which is what makes builder code read like a DSL. Trailing lambda syntax works for any function type, so that is not the reason. Receiver lambdas follow normal visibility rules, so they cannot see private members.

questions.question: Why does this declaration not compile?
options: Extension properties must be declared `var`, because they are compiled to a getter and setter pair
`this` cannot be used in an extension property; the receiver is only available in extension functions
Extension properties are only allowed on classes you own, and `String` is a final class from the stdlib
Extension properties have no backing field, so they can't have an initializer; use a getter instead
questions.explanation: An extension cannot add state to an existing class, so there is no field to initialize. The fix is `val String.firstChar: Char get() = this[0]`, which is computed on every access. `this` is available in extension property getters, and extensions work on final classes such as `String`.
